newsitem.title: UK: U.S/UK relations to improve under Blair - Jackson.
newsitem.headline: U.S/UK relations to improve under Blair - Jackson.

text.p: Anglo-U.S. relations are bound to improve if opposition Labour leader Tony Blair wins next month's British election, dual Hollywood Oscar winner turned Labour politician Glenda Jackson said on Monday.
"That relationship is clearly one that is more than merely cordial," she said of the links between Blair and U.S. President Bill Clinton.
Ties were strengthened by a visit to Washington last April by Blair, the opinion poll favourite to win the May 1 election.
Unlike Ronald Reagan's warm admiration for then Conservative premier Margaret Thatcher, relations between Clinton and Prime Minister John Major are merely businesslike.
Labour aides gave steady help to Clinton's re-election campaign last year, in sharp contrast to Conservative backing of President George Bush in his failed 1992 re-election bid.

Jackson told reporters: "It is hardly surprising that relations between the U.S. and the present British government are bad given that the Conservative Party sent over people to actively work against Clinton during the first election."

She said Blair and Clinton shared a similar approach to world problems. "You certainly have a similarity of age...and there are many similarities in the kind of world they would both like to see begin to emerge."
Jackson, who has no regrets about turning her back on the world of acting, is defending her constituency in the fashionable London suburb of Hampstead against four women candidates.
"I think it is really terrific," she said with feeling after five years working in the House of Commons, which is permeated by the "Old Boys Network" atmosphere of a London club.

"It is surely scandalous and disgraceful that the number of women MPs in what is, I believe, somewhat ironically called the Mother of Parliaments, are still less than 10 percent," she told a news conference called especially for international media.

They were fascinated to know why Jackson turned her back on the glitzy world of showbusiness for the 18-hour daily grind of working in parliament as junior transport spokeswoman for a party out of power for almost two decades.
Jackson, a bricklayer's daughter who won Oscars for the D.H. Lawrence classic "Women in Love" and the comedy "A Touch of Class", clearly feels she now has her priorities right.
"I do think the creation of a government at this stage in our country's history after 18 years of virtually one-party government...is somewhat more important than any theatrical production.
"But I must be honest. When I was engaged in such theatrical productions, they did comprise the sum total of my known world at the time."

Jackson, a pallid and gaunt figure who is stridently unglamorous, gave her mother the two Oscars to use as doorstops and spent much of her stage career playing forceful women like Cleopatra and Elizabeth I.
She shares two traits with Thatcher -- they are workaholics who fervently believe in conviction politics.
But the similarities end there, with Jackson freely admitting that fury over Thatcher brought her into the political frontline.
"What enraged me and caused me to walk into my closed French windows, almost breaking my nose, was when Mad Margaret said there was no such thing as society. That to me was the final straw."
